lesson.title: Programmed Cell Death: A Cell's Planned Demolition
lesson.summary: Apoptosis is a tightly regulated, energy-dependent program of cell suicide that removes damaged, unneeded, or dangerous cells without harming their neighbors, in sharp contrast to the uncontrolled cell death of necrosis.
lesson.body:
When a cell needs to be eliminated, whether because it is damaged, no longer needed, or potentially dangerous, the body has a controlled way to do it: apoptosis, or programmed cell death. Apoptosis is often described in contrast to necrosis, the other main way cells die. Necrosis is what happens when a cell is damaged so severely, by injury, infection, or lack of oxygen, that it loses control of its own membrane and simply swells and bursts, spilling its contents into the surrounding tissue and triggering inflammation. Apoptosis is the opposite in almost every way: it is an active, energy-requiring program the cell carries out on itself in an orderly sequence. The cell shrinks rather than swells, its chromatin condenses and its DNA is cut into fragments, and the cell eventually breaks apart into small, membrane-bound pieces called apoptotic bodies. Because those pieces stay enclosed in membrane the whole time, neighboring phagocytic cells can engulf and clear them without ever spilling cellular contents into the tissue, so apoptosis, unlike necrosis, does not trigger inflammation.

The machinery that carries out this program is a family of enzymes called caspases, proteases that are normally kept inactive until a cell receives a signal to die. Caspases work as a cascade: initiator caspases are activated first in response to a death signal, and their job is to cleave and activate executioner caspases, which then cut apart structural proteins in the cytoskeleton and nucleus, producing the shrinking, blebbing, and DNA fragmentation that define apoptosis under a microscope. This cascade structure means a relatively small initiating signal gets converted into a fast, committed execution of the cell, much like the signal transduction pathways that relay other cellular signals, except that here the end result is the controlled disassembly of the cell itself rather than a change in gene expression or metabolism.

Cells can be pushed into apoptosis through two main routes. In the extrinsic pathway, a death signaling molecule outside the cell, such as Fas ligand, binds a death receptor on the cell's surface, and that binding event recruits adaptor proteins inside the cell that activate an initiator caspase. That is a direct example of signal transduction: an external signal received at the membrane is relayed inward through a defined chain of protein interactions to produce a specific cellular outcome. In the intrinsic, or mitochondrial, pathway, internal stress such as severe DNA damage or growth factor withdrawal causes mitochondria to release cytochrome c into the cytoplasm, where it assembles with other proteins into a complex that activates a different initiator caspase. Both pathways converge on the same executioner caspases and the same final outcome.

Apoptosis is not a backup system the body uses only when something goes wrong, it is a routine and essential part of normal biology. During development, apoptosis sculpts tissues by removing cells that are no longer needed, such as the webbing of cells between what will become individual fingers in an embryonic hand. Throughout life, it removes cells with damaged DNA that might otherwise become cancerous, and it helps regulate the immune system by eliminating immune cells that are no longer required once an infection is cleared. Because apoptosis is so central to keeping the right cells alive and removing the wrong ones, failures in this program have serious consequences: cells that should die but resist apoptosis can accumulate mutations and progress toward cancer, while excessive or misdirected apoptosis is linked to degenerative conditions in which healthy cells are lost.
